source: Whisper large-v3-turbo (mlx-whisper), edited for punctuation, casing, and speaker turns

paragraphs.text: Welcome back to another episode of Tis the Podcast. The podcast that has determined to keep the spirit of Christmas alive 365 days a year. A job that is getting much, much easier. I'm Thom. I'm Julia. And I'm Anthony. So I'm going to be honest, guys, as we get going. I was not very excited to do this movie, but I got obsessed with researching it and I'm looking forward to the talk. What movie are we talking about, Thom? We are talking about 1984's Gremlins, which was, interestingly enough, released the same day as Ghostbusters. Julia, do you want to read the synopsis for us?

Three rules. Billy had only three rules for the Mogwai. An early Christmas present from his father bought at a super shady Chinese curiosity shop. Do not expose it to bright lights or sunlight, which will kill it. Do not let it get wet and never feed it after midnight. When Billy can't follow these very simple rules, the cuddly little gizmo spawns an army of demons that wreak havoc on Kingston Falls, leaving a trail of bodies and damage in their wake. Good synopsis. Did you write that, Thom? I did.

I don't know that there's a time I don't remember this movie. Gizmo was so super cute in the '80s. I think Julia can attest, we all wanted little Gizmo dolls. They had them. It was definitely marketed toward kids. When I did see the movie, it was not at all as cute and cuddly as I had thought it would be. I remember Gizmo before I saw the movie, and then I remember the movie, and I'm like, what is happening here? It kind of blew my mind. And it's a movie I don't think I've watched since the mid-'80s, to be perfectly honest, until today. How about you, Julia?

So I've never not known this movie to be around, but I realized today when I watched it that I've never seen this movie. I've seen bits and pieces of it, apparently, but when I was watching it, I was like, I remember none of this, except for a few bits and pieces. So that was interesting. I feel like lots of '80s movies are like that for me. But it's a Steven Spielberg movie, so I had a lot of fun watching it.
Written by Chris Columbus, too.
Yeah, right. So I'm really excited to talk about it this week. How about you, Anthony? Did you see it after it had been out for ten years, when you were six years old?

So my history with this movie is, I vividly remember the VHS box for the second Gremlins, over this first one. And it had one of the gremlins themselves on it, not one of the mogwai. I don't know if Spike's in the second one or not, I haven't seen Gremlins 2, but he looked like him, and he was sitting in a chair overlooking Manhattan. I remember that box vividly growing up.
It's funny, you just described that box and I knew exactly what you were talking about.
Yeah, me too. I have that memory.

I mean, it was clearly a memorable image. But I think I saw Gremlins 2 first, actually. That one was definitely more family-friendly. Not that this one isn't, but that one was a lot more slapsticky. But I saw this movie pretty young, and I really liked it growing up. Gizmo was cute. I really liked him. And it was a kid on an adventure with his cute pet, and his dog, too.
I love this dog.

I do too. And his cute girlfriend. So I was a big fan of this movie growing up. I haven't seen it in years. I was aware it was still around. A few years ago, you'd see the commercials for the new Gizmo version of the Furby, which I feel is very meta, because Furby had to have been inspired by Gremlins. And I have a Gizmo ornament in a Santa hat for my Christmas tree. But yeah, this is the first time I've watched it in years, and I really enjoyed it, and I'm looking forward to talking about it with you guys.

I am too. Well, real quick, I'll do the obligatory credits. It was written by Chris Columbus, who we've discussed extensively in previous episodes. It was directed by Joe Dante, who did Gremlins 2: The New Batch, Small Soldiers, and Looney Tunes: Back in Action.

Steven Spielberg is the producer, and he almost chose Tim Burton because he really liked Tim Burton's short films. He was concerned that Tim Burton had not yet directed a full-length film, so he passed Tim Burton up and went with Joe Dante. And then Tim Burton went on to do Batman. Could you imagine a Tim Burton Gremlins? I feel like it would have been a little bit creepy. I think it would have been a hard R and would not be anywhere near family friendly. I think that scene, I read about a scene they had originally in the script where the Gremlins go into McDonald's and start eating people.
Tim Burton would have kept that. That would have been so Tim Burton. With like the plastic artificial colors of McDonald's and the darkness of gremlins eating people inside of it.

I want to watch that movie. So the cast, Zach Galligan plays Billy Peltzer. He was in some ABC after school specials. He returned to Gremlins 2, was in Hellraiser 3, Hell on Earth. And then he had a lot of guest appearances on TV shows like Dr. Quinn Medicine Woman, Love Boat. Star Trek Voyager, Seventh Heaven, Law and Order, Criminal Intent. Phoebe Cates played Kate Beringer, his love interest. I really remembered her from Fast Times at Ridgemont High. I don't know if you guys were big fans of that movie, but I sure was. And Drop Dead Fred, which I also remember.

Hoyt Axton played Billy's dad, Rand Peltzer. He's an Oklahoma boy, from Duncan, Oklahoma. He had some roles in TV shows like Growing Pains and In the Heat of the Night. He was in a big Civil War miniseries, and on Murder, She Wrote, Diff'rent Strokes, and Bonanza. And I found this interesting: he wrote "Joy to the World" for Three Dog Night. You know that song?
Yeah. "Joy to the World," that one?

Yep. And I was just amazed at how many movies and shows it's been in, including TV Christmas episodes. That song has been featured in Last Man on Earth, Sausage Party, iZombie, The Christmas Chronicles, Tropic Thunder, My Name Is Earl, Malcolm in the Middle, American Idol, The X-Files, 28 Days, Sex and the City, Forrest Gump, Encino Man, Roger & Me, Designing Women, and The Big Chill.

And that's just, that's a condensed list. So Hoyt definitely left his mark on TV. Francis Lee McCain as Lynn Peltzer. She played Marty McFly's mom's mom on Back to the Future. She was in Footloose, Stand By Me, Patch Adams, Scream, and had guest appearances on TV shows like Diagnosis Murder, Father Dowling Mysteries, Dallas, Alfred Hitchcock Presents, Walt Disney's Wonderful World of Color, Bob Newhart Show, The Rockford Files, Three's Company, and St. Elsewhere.
For any of you born in the 80s, Corey Feldman needs no introduction. He played Pete Fontaine.

He was in Friday the 13th, A New Beginning, Stand By Me, The Lost Boys, The Berg's. I did not know he was the voice of Donatello in Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles 1, 3, and the cartoon. I didn't either. He was in Tales from the Crypt, Bordello of Blood.
And he was in The Fox and the Hound as one of the voices. And last, Howie Mandel is the voice of Gizmo. I did not know that. I really loved his dramatic reading of, Break late, break late.

I just, this movie, the more I learned, the more I started researching, the bigger the rabbit hole went. I do feel we'd be remiss if we didn't mention that a Christmas movie alum is also in this movie, and that would be Judge Reinhold as Gerald Hopkins. He was. He was. He had a small part, right? Right, he did. He worked at the bank. And was a total, total jerk. Yeah, he was. A far cry from Neil. A far cry from the kind, patient Neil.
But I did laugh when I saw him, and he was bullying Billy, talking about how much money he was making at 23.
Okay, he did not look 23. Maybe he was.

All right, so the movie opens, and you see Billy's dad, Rand, following some young Asian boy into a scary, sketchy alley and going down into a curio shop run by this boy's grandfather. And, I mean, there's weird stuff in here. His dad tries pitching the old man a travel kit that has everything you need when you travel.
And he comes across a mogwe, which in Cantonese is like a devil or demon.
And the grandfather refuses to sell it to him. He says it takes too much responsibility.
The grandson decides, hey, money's money. He sells it to him and gives him the three rules that Julia read. Rand takes the mogwai, who becomes Gizmo, home, and that's how we start our movie.
I was remarkably surprised by how little shocked reaction people had when meeting Gizmo. This strange foreign creature. Like, what the heck is this thing?
Yeah. It's an entirely new species. Let me buy it and take it home.
Let's take our picture with it. This is what I wanted for my son.
Also, the '80s were a different time. The blatantly racist stereotype of the grandfather.
Lord, it was. Wow. It felt blatantly racist.
So let's go through and discuss what we liked and didn't like about the movie. And I want to kick that off with one thing I do have to say about this film: it feels like Christmas.
It does.

Everywhere you look, it looks like Christmas. They chose wonderful Christmas music throughout the entire film, even during the creepy scenes. It would be a really slowed-down, pitched-down Christmas song, but everything in it definitely had a Christmas vibe and feel.

Well, even after that opening scene with the grandfather, to transition from that creepy basement with this weird creature, they do a montage with such an upbeat Christmas song, as we're seeing the village square and snow and everything. I really liked that hard transition.
Which, by the way, is the same village square from Back to the Future. The same town, everything, from Back to the Future.
Yep. The theater at the end that blows up was the theater that Marty McFly crashed into, and the same theater that burned down in Back to the Future Part III.
Oh my gosh, that is so cool.
When I read that, I'm like, wait, was it really? And I went and looked at screenshots of Back to the Future. Wow. That is such a cool connection.
What scenes did you guys like? What really stuck out to you?

So I really love the scene where the gremlins are trying to murder the mother in the kitchen, and Mom just takes a knife and takes one out. She puts one in one of Dad's… Oh yeah, the other thing that we need to mention, for those of you who haven't seen it: Rand is a really terrible inventor who makes a bunch of products that we see throughout the entire film, as little moments of humor, that just don't work. Like, Billy tries to make orange juice in a juicer, and one little orange ends up exploding. I don't know how one orange could have that much liquid, but it was funny. And she ends up getting one of the gremlins into Dad's blender, and you just see the feet flopping around. She puts one of them in the microwave, and you watch it heating up and looking curious, and then its head explodes.
It reminds me of… do you remember that hamster-in-a-blender, or hamster-in-the-microwave, thing?

It was like an internet deal where you'd push the buttons and he would like cuss at you and get mad. Yeah, I remember that. Like probably like 1999 to 2001. And they had the frog in the blender too. They had also, this scene they cut down for violence and disturbing imagery. Because at one point she stabs a gremlin through the chest. and originally they had they spent all this money on an animatronic of this poor gremlin trying to remove the knife from his chest and they cut it because that was too disturbing for kids but you can see him trying to do it in the background of the shot oh my god I liked it when that awful Mrs. I can't even think of her name got it with the electric chair the up and down Mrs. Dingle when she got it.

That whole scene where she meets her demise just reinforced what I said the other week about how horror movies turn me into a terrible person. I was cackling with glee the entire time. Oh my god. She is such a wicked witch wannabe too. I'll get that dog.
She's terrible. 100% reference back to the Wizard of Oz on that one.
I'm going to deviate here a little bit. You said it was a horror movie. Do we all think this was a horror movie?
I'd call it a comedy.
That's what the label says.
I know it is. That's why I'm asking. I don't know what to call it.
The label technically says comedy horror.

Okay, I can agree with that. If there's a downgraded version of horror, that would be it, you know what I mean? It's kind of an introduction to horror for younger kids. So this is how I can traumatize my child at an early age before going all in.

And it's especially diabolical, because you get reeled in with a super precious and adorable Gizmo. And it was supposed to be even more traumatizing, because the original script had Gizmo turning into Spike. And then they decided they needed at least one good mogwai, because he's so cute, so they kept Gizmo and made Spike a separate character.
That would have been awful.
Terrible, if they had done that.
When water gets on Gizmo, he's in pain, and these little fur balls pop out.
Tribbles. They're totally tribbles.
These tribbles pop out, and they become new mogwai. Only the second generation of them all have an evil streak that Gizmo does not.
It's the whole "you can't make a copy of a copy" kind of thing, right? Which this isn't, a copy of a copy, but I think it's that idea.
Yeah. Gizmo is pure, and the duplicates are not. From the get-go, they're just bad.
Yeah, they are. Okay, but I like the design of them when they become the gremlins. I like that contrast between Gizmo and Spike. I thought both of their designs were really, really good.
Spike's mohawk.
Yeah, the mohawk, totally. So you know he's bad. You know he's bad, because he has a mohawk.
Yes. A fluffy white mohawk.
A scene I really did not like: I hated the bar scene.
Yeah, the one with Kate at the beginning?

No, no, no. When all the gremlins go to the bar, and they're harassing Kate, and she's, for whatever reason, still serving these gremlins drinks. They're obviously not going to pay you. You leave, right? But where did they get gremlin-sized wigs? Like the one at the poker table with a wig and makeup. Perfect lipstick. That was a stretch. They were trying to be too schticky for me, and it failed miserably.
So can we talk about Kate for a moment? Because hands down, she has the most depressing Santa Claus story ever.
That is in my favorite quotes, but not because it's a favorite.
Me too. It was in the script, and they wanted to cut it, but the director fought to keep it. Steven Spielberg didn't like it, because he didn't know if it was supposed to be funny or sad.
I'll read it.
Can you set the scene, where they are, and what she says to get Billy to ask the question?

They go into the school, and they're trying to track Spike down, and he's obviously wreaked havoc, and she says, "Now I have another reason to hate Christmas." And Billy says, "What are you talking about?"
[Reads Kate's monologue from the film about how she found out there was no Santa Claus.]
I'm sorry. I'm a horrible person.
That's how I took it too. I thought we were supposed to find it kind of ridiculous and funny. Not... Oh, man.
Oh, boy. For any aspiring theater students out there, if you want to do that as a monologue, good luck getting through it without laughing.
I would pay to see a dramatic interpretation of that.
Despite her sob story, though, I really did like the character of Kate. She was pitiful. I just felt bad for her in every interaction, until she found her courage at the end.
How did you like the neighbor who lived next door to Billy? The guy who was obsessed with his American-made car, and the gremlins drove it through his house?
Well, he was the same guy who was obsessed with gremlins, right?
Yeah. He was talking about them while he was drunk at the beginning.

Yeah, yeah. And he's like, "Gremlins in the cab." Okay. So when the cops get there, they're like, oh, there was a freak accident with the snowplow in his house. I don't know how a snowplow accidentally turns on and drives into a house and crushes somebody.
So what is it with cops in Christmas horror movies? Because they were as useless as the cops in Black Christmas.
I don't know. Inept cops.
But the neighbor was in your favorite movie ever, Julia. He was the coach in Grease.
Was he really?
Any other favorite scenes? Anybody?
I liked… so, didn't Spielberg do The Goonies?
Yes.

So I like how, at least in these two instances, you have a family that's very close-knit, with a somewhat inept inventor included. In The Goonies, you have Data, and Data and his dad are both inventors, and you see that really well when they reunite at the end. The whole time, you see that Data is an inventor. He's got all these quirky little inventions, and half the time they don't work that great. And at the end, his dad pulls out a quirky invention that doesn't work that great. So I kind of liked that.
I love The Goonies.

And that made me think about this, probably the Spielberg thing also. But I liked how the mom and the son weren't put off by the dad's failures, right? You didn't get that feeling at all. I don't know.

Yeah. It wasn't negative at all. They were a little frustrated, but they loved him and you could tell that. And that made me very happy. Yeah, me too. It would have been the easy a cliche route to have them be frustrated with him. To view him as a failure.
Which he was.
Yes, but they loved him. A failure surrounded by support.
I really liked the end of this movie. If we're talking about favorite scenes, they're Billy and Gizmo's goodbye.
I just thought it was very sweet. Gizmo was so sweet at that point.

I like the homage they had to other movies like phone home reference when Spike tells her phone home. Oh, and when they show at the beginning of the film, when they show the movie theater, it has two movies on there. One is A Boy's Life and one is Watch the Skies, which were the working titles for E.T. and Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Hey, that's cool. That's really neat. I could have sworn, too, one of the signs looked like the radioactive sign that you see in Back to the Future when Marty McFly is in the yellow radiation suit and he gets out. And I know that made me think of Back to the Future. And I was trying to find these things because I knew it was Spielberg. and I'm like, he has to have dropped Easter eggs.
It could have been intentional, especially since it was shot in the back of the future town and everything.
So did you know that they initially tried to get monkeys and masks to play the gremlins and the animal went crazy and tore apart their office and desiccated everywhere?
Oh my gosh.
In fairness, genius I did get a monkey since they're little troublemakers, but I don't know how they thought they could control them. How can we get a monkey? Let's put a monkey in a helmet.
That's going to turn out well.
So you're speaking of Steven Spielberg's Christmas Eggs. One of Chris Columbus's, just like in Home Alone 1 and 2, on the TV, they had It's a Wonderful Life playing.
Good old It's a Wonderful Life. We're going to have to cover that movie.
I think that has to be saved for around Christmastime.
I think we should do it next year. '19.
Yep.

So I mentioned earlier how Gizmo was originally intended to turn into Stripe. They initially thought he wouldn't be in the movie very much, so they designed the puppet to not be as functional as all the gremlins, and this poor animatronic kept breaking down on set, frustrating the filmmakers. So the scene where they hang him on a dartboard and throw darts at him came from a list the filmmakers drew up, called "Horrible Things to Do to Gizmo," because they hated that puppet so much. They just had a list of ways for the gremlins to torture the puppet.
Puppets were awful in the '80s, weren't they? Did you guys watch that show Dinosaurs?
Yes. I watched a single episode of it and then swore never to make that mistake again.
Really? I watched it as a kid.
Obnoxious.

No, I hated the ending, where they went extinct. Seriously. It ended with the ice age basically happening, snow falling, because of a big chemical plant, basically their own doing. And they're all in the house saying, "Are we going to be okay?" as the snow's piling up on the ground outside. And that's how the show ended.
Yeah. It's sick.
I know. Oh my God, that's awful.
Something about the mogwai, maybe it was their eyes, reminded me of Dinosaurs.
I can see that. The eyelids, shuddering.
Kind of reminded me of the Furby. It had to be inspired by these things, right?
It had to be. They're Furbies.
Yeah. Had to be.
Our dog Tucker, when he was a puppy, everybody said he looked like Gizmo. That was almost his name. He looked just like Gizmo. So cute.
So Marty was called Gizmo for a while after this movie came out, because his brothers all thought he looked like Gizmo.
You should bring it back.
He told me that earlier, and I'm like, that's coming up tonight.
All right. That would be cool.

I think it would be, compared to what you could be called. But growing up, when I had a Furby, those things went off at all hours of the night. When I was really young and had one, they made noises. They were motion-activated.
Oh, I never had one.
My dad always warned me, "Don't feed it after midnight," because that thing would wake up begging for food. You had to feed it.
Well, yeah. Like a Tamagotchi pet.
But basically, you stuck your finger in its mouth, and it would nibble on your finger.
Oh, it's horrifying.
Hey, Furbies are terrifying. Have you ever seen them without their skin on? The exoskeleton? They're terrifying.
No, I've never skinned a Furby.
Oh, they are terrifying. They are so scary. Oh my gosh. They're basically what a Furby would morph into if you fed him after midnight.
Probably. That's the stuff nightmares are made of, right there.
Anyway, I think we should move on to the question. Do you guys think this is a Christmas movie?

For the Christmas feels, the vibes, all that, I do. But the story itself is not Christmas. There's no overarching Linus moment. This is a great, awesome family when we start, and they're a great, awesome family when we end. There's no real growth. As much as I don't want to, I have to say maybe.

I'm going with a hard no for all those same reasons. And I keep using Die Hard as sort of a litmus test for movies like this. What I was missing here was exactly what that whole Linus moment, right? Like how you said they're a good family to start off with and end up as a good family. Like John McClane realized, you know, he put his priorities straight and he sacrificed his life to do it. And it was Christmas season. And I don't feel like this movie allowed for that. So while it was beautiful scenery wise and it did give me the happy Christmas feels, it was not a Christmas movie to me. What I hear is Julia saying, I wanted a dysfunctional family and they let me down.

She wanted them to be horrible to the father. That's what's so funny though is I'm so glad they weren't. That made me really happy, but not happy enough to think it's a Christmas movie. You know what I mean? I'm going with a hard yes it is. For exactly the same reasons you are. It has as much Christmas for me as in Die Hard in terms of the scenery it takes place at Christmas. It doesn't have the Linus moment, but a lot of the movies we covered on our list that are Christmas movies don't have Linus moments, including Muppets Family Christmas, which will end in our top 10, which we said that's one of the first overtly Christmas movies we had that didn't have it. So I would argue it didn't need the Linus moment to be a Christmas movie.
It had everything else.
And I'm going to say yes, it was.
So we fell with a yes, a no, and a maybe. Nothing conclusive.
Nothing. Well, we did ask our listeners, but they didn't help us.

Okay, so were we splitsville? Between Twitter, Facebook, Reddit, and Instagram, we had 135 people weigh in, and the consensus was 85 people saying yes, it's a Christmas movie, and 50 people saying no, it's not. So according to our listeners, it is a Christmas movie.
I just have a really hard time with this one. I'm having a hard time landing, even.
Okay, let's ask this. Do you think it's more Christmas than Batman Returns?
Yes. But Batman Returns was woefully not Christmas.
Yeah. I would say it's more Christmas than Batman Returns.
See, I don't know. Maybe it's just me.
So 59% said yes, right? You said 85 of them?
85 across all of our social media said yes, and 50 said no.

I found myself also comparing it to Krampus while I was watching it, since we have a small number of Christmas-type horror and scary films. And I think, even if you take the Santa part out of Krampus, the way the family grows through it, it's undeniable that Krampus is a Christmas movie. It's the growth that was lacking for me.
I feel like Krampus was made to be a Christmas movie, right?

Right, it was. It's not a perfect comparison, but if we're talking about underlying family growth, that's what was missing for me. That's it. Now, all that to say, I will probably watch this movie around Christmas every year. I'm going to make it a point to do that now, because it was a lot of fun, the scenery is on point, and it had some really good holiday stuff in it.
See, where I landed on it was, this is going to be an October movie for me.
Oh, really?
That's where I landed. I was like, this is going to be an October movie for me.

Well, I'm going to be contrary and say this is going to be a November movie for me. I like the horror aspect. It gives me something fun that's innocent and good to watch during October, like a good Halloween movie you can watch with the family.
See, I consider this more Christmas and horror. I see it as a build-up to Christmas for me. It's like a transition period.

Yeah. I mean, most of the parts with the gremlins have nothing to do with Christmas, aside from trying to strangle her with tinsel and stuff like that. Most of the bulk of the gremlin stuff, like the bar scene, which I didn't like, or the movie theater, has nothing to do with Christmas.
The dog looked beautiful, strung up in lights.
Oh, he said the dog looked beautiful strung up in Christmas lights. That was really upsetting to me.
That was upsetting to me too. But the way they had him, he was safe. He wasn't in danger.
Well, no, I don't mean the filming. I'm sure he was fine with the filming. I mean just thinking about it.
I know. Were the gremlins the ones that did it?
Yes, I assume, because Stripe was on that shelf giggling.
Oh, right, right.
But I don't know. I just didn't like that. It's very uneasy. I really like that dog.
I loved when he hopped over the bank counter, when Mrs. Deagle, or whatever her name was, was complaining about him, and he broke her snowman's head. He was a really good actor dog.
The gremlins were watching Snow White, which, they commented, was a Christmas-release Disney movie.
Okay, all right. I wondered. I don't like Snow White, by the way. My least favorite Disney movie of all time.
Any of the old ones?
No. I like Cinderella. I hate Sleeping Beauty. I hate Snow White.
Oh, I love Cinderella. I love Sleeping Beauty.
I hate Snow White.
The dwarves are so cute, though. I love Dopey and Grumpy.
I like them all. Dopey, Grumpy, Papa Smurf, all of them.
So, favorite quotes?
Yes, I have a few.
Go ahead, Anthony.
You've already read one of them. That was amazing.
I already read one that had me in stitches. We should make it.
I liked when Kate said, you say you hate Washington's birthday or Thanksgiving and nobody cares, but you say you hate Christmas and people treat you like you're a leper.
Anthony, look at this. These are my first two favorite quotes I have. I'm screenshotting this to you.
We are still on the same page tonight. That makes two weeks in a row. What is going on with us?
I don't know. But yeah, those were the first two quotes I had.
I love that quote, and she's right. When you say you hate Christmas, I treat you like a leper too. I don't trust somebody who doesn't love Christmas.

So I thought it was hilarious when the dad was at that conference, on the phone talking to his wife, and Robby the Robot is behind him on the other side of the booth. It's the most random thing ever. You just hear snippets of what he says, and he goes, "Sorry, miss, I was giving myself an oil job." "This question is totally without meaning."

"Pardon me, sir." "Stuff?" "Thick and heavy?" "Would 60 gallons be sufficient?" "I rarely use it myself, sir. It promotes rust." Because every time the dad said something, he would respond to it. Man, it made me laugh. I'm sure it was supposed to be completely inappropriate, but I thought it was funny.
This isn't so much a favorite quote as something that really annoyed me: when Mrs. Deagle goes in and tells Billy, "I want your dog."
I had that one too. It was on the same page.

She goes, "Give him to me. I'll take him to the kennel. They'll put him to sleep. It'll be quick and painless, compared to what I would do to him." Billy decides to provoke her and says, "What could you do?" "I'll catch the beast myself. He'll get what he deserves. A slow, painful death."

"Maybe I'll put him in my spin dryer on high heat." And then some random guy listening just says, "That would do it." All right. Who's going to sit by and listen to a woman tell a teenage kid that she wants to put his dog in a dryer, and agree with her? "Yep, that would do the trick." Nobody called this lady out at all.
Nowadays, I'd be livestreaming that to Facebook, like, "Keep talking, lady. Monetize."

I like when, at the end, the grandfather comes to get Gizmo, and he says, "You do with mogwai what your society has done with all of nature's gifts. You do not understand. You are not ready." But I like how he left it open that maybe one day you will be. Because Gizmo is obviously sad to leave Billy, and Billy's sad to see Gizmo go.
And I have another one that no one else has.
I just had "Caca." I don't know why Spike kept saying "caca."

I liked the narration at the end, from the neighbor: "So if your air conditioner goes on the fritz, or your washing machine blows up, or your video recorder conks out, before you call the repairman, turn on all the lights, check all the closets and cupboards, look under all the beds. 'Cause you never can tell. There just might be a gremlin in your house."
That neighbor was crazy.
Julia, any more from you?
